title: Eternal Sunshine Of The Spotless Mind, How Cruel Love Can Be

commenti.body:
I’m glad to see this post. I did a ten year ish re watch last month and I really loved it. 

I’m biased because I am a huge fan of Kaufmans writing. I loved it. It’s really hard to write what it is about the movie that is so interesting but I think ultimately it’s the portrayal of love and regret. The moment when you see the real first meeting was so emotionally heavy. It seems like in the ending they decided to date again but the last shot to me signifies that their relationship ended again and they decided to just enjoy their bad memories instead of try to erase them and repeat them.

I’d say ultimately the movie was kind of a portrait of that one relationship that made you feel true love but it ultimately never worked out for reasons that seem cosmically out of your control. 

I am curious, so the first time they met was not that house they broke into but Joel decided to leave? Do we just assume they stayed in contact after that? 

Also my other lingering thing was lots of people online seemed to decide that there was a mistake with the process of the memory wiping or maybe it couldn’t wipe everything. My interpretation was that the process could wipe memories but it couldn’t wipe emotions or the innate feelings people have about each other.

Charlie Kaufman is a genius writer no doubt about it. Love and regret I'd agree are a big theme to this film and how people struggle to move on from a relationship and longing for the good days of a failing relationship, it's quite poignant.

I think we agree on the ending, you have to grow as a person, we need painful experiences in our lives in order to learn from them.

Unless I'm missing something it seems like that they first met at the beach house, we see Joel going to see here at the bookstore too when he apologises which I presume was for him leaving her there.

I'd agree that the process is successful and emotion is the reason they meet again. This is a fantastic film with so many layers.

I think it’s a very sad ending. Similar to avoiding a hot stove because you’ve learned that you’ll get burned, we learn who to seek and who to avoid based on previous relationships, good and bad. Pain is a necessary part of learning and unfortunately for them, they live in a world where they can choose to remove that pain, thus never having to learn. The final shot with Joel and Clementine running through the beach, the shot continuously skipping cements this for me. They’re doomed to repeat their mistakes, never learning from their pain.

I completely overlooked the skips at the end but that is a really good point, that makes the ending even sadder not to mention that Mary gave them the opportunity to end the cycle. Love does strange things to us.

I really like your reading of the ending. I loved this film, but always hated the ending. I haven't seen it in a bit, but I interpreted the ending as even though they may never work out as a couple, they are star-crossed lovers and fate will always bring them together even if their memories are erased. They choose to repeatedly be in a relationship that is doomed to fail because they rather have the brief fated "true love" that will inevitably deteriorate than settle for someone they can have a practical relationship.


I don't know why I interpreted it that way, but I always found that to be too romantic and saccharine for my tastes. I'll have to rewatch it with your interpretation in mind.

So much talk of pain and strife and how it's sad. Like the comment about the ending quote "doomed to repear their mistakes".

This misses what I think the fundamental point of the film

Why Joel says 'Enjoy it." At the beach house.

The film's message is ultimately, better to have loved and lost than never loved at all. Any pain or negative emotions are ultimately outweighed by the positives of being in love.

While there are moments that are definitely depressing, existential, the ending is beautiful and even uplifting.

I agree with your take but it is quite open to interpretation. I really love the ending like when Joel says "Ok", that's quite nice after how much this film has played with our emotions. Love is a strange feeling.

Sure, it's open insofar that you take it to be a good thing and be joyful or a bad thing and be doom and gloom.

But I see it as quite cut and dry as for the film's thesis. If you just follow the character arcs and the ending itself.

I watched it the first time recently and didn't do much. Good enough to watch through and some strong moments for sure, but I wasn't strongly gripped emotionally nor replaying it in my mind afterwards. 

Was wondering if there's some Seinfeld is Unfunny effect, or some backstory from when it came out to make it resonate so strongly?

My mistake may also be unwillingly comparing it to Being John Malovitch, which was incredible to me.

Read the essay “Personal Identity”  by Derek Parfit. It will give you a new appreciation for the movie. The horror of the movie is not just that he’s losing good memories - it’s that by erasing his memories he’s losing bits and pieces of himself. What he has done is, in a sense, commit suicide.
I'm not familiar with it but I am with Camus who I think would have a similar view
the director tho I didnt know he wrote&shot Sunshine and Science of sleep and Be kind Rewind back to back lol
Just wanted to say that I agree with you. Not sure how it could be interpreted a different way.

Same. I'm similar to both protagonists so I was in a good mindset starting it. By 20mins I noticed a lot of bad editing decisions and didn't really enjoy the rest of the film, especially with the strange doctor subplot.

I feel like it's more the romanticization of 2 off kilter people falling in love in the city that people are fond of. Because tbf, it's perfect subject matter for a love story but I didn't feel it
I agree with you. People trying to paint it almost horror film is a bit weird.

> I am curious, so the first time they met was not that house they broke into but Joel decided to leave? Do we just assume they stayed in contact after that? 

Isn't it that they broke into the house and he left, but then their next meeting is at the bookstore/library where she works so he can ask her out?

One of my all time favorite films. This movie messed with me so hard, specially because when I was going through a heartbreak, but ultimately the ending is so uplifting that I can't help but laugh with Joel and Clementine.


What I love about this movie is that it not only shows you the agony of reliving past memories and how we can have nostalgic goggles or tinted eyes, but it ultimately tries to convey that loss is just part of life and just because you're no longer with someone doesn't mean you have to forget about the personal growth you did during that time. When you're in a relationship with someone it's not just about getting to know you significant other more. You also get to know yourself a little more. You find out what you're willing to do for them and how their presence makes you better (after all there's a reason you chose to be with them in the first place).


The filmmaking is absolutely brilliant. The way the writing places all these twists and turns feels natural. Even though Clem's relationship with Patrick feels a bit rushed, it could also be seen as a cautionary tale of what happens when you rush and force a relationship. The cinematography and the editing are incredible. The way it's shot always kinda reminded me of _AMERICAN HISTORY X_ for some reason.

Came here to also comment on the final shot of them running on the beach, played on a loop, implying that they meet again and repeat the procedure often. Fated to find one another over and over again. Heartbreaking.

I took the ending to be similar to the Molly Bloom “Yes” soliloquy in James Joyce’s Ulysses. 

They know they are going to cause each other pain, and they are still choosing to do it all over again. 

That seems hopeful to me. That is a grown up love story and not a cloying happy ending Hollywood movie. The good parts are better than the bad parts of life. And the bad parts of life help is appreciate the good parts even more. 

Most romantic movies focus on a single instance of overcoming a bad part of a relationship and then they live happily ever after with only good times to follow. Wouldn’t it be pretty to think so?

Did Joel and Clementine learn anything? Sure they could repeat the same mistakes time and time again but with Mary sending them their tapes could they actually accept that their relationship is doomed but it's ok because they are both an important part in each others lives. Sure it will be painful but is love not worth the pain?

However maybe they don't want to grow and want to keep their fantasy of each other alive and repeating the procedure allows them to do that, I feel sorry for Joel's friends in that case.

Either way I think it's more complicated than joyful or gloomy, it can be both at the same time and still be rewarding.
